name: Operating Systems
blurb: One best video per subtopic, chosen for correct, interview-depth explanations, with a deeper lecture and a quicker or more visual alternative. Watch the best pick, then do that subtopic's MCQs.
method:
• Best pick: the clearest correct explanation at interview depth, usually 10–30 minutes. Most come from Mythili Vutukuru's IIT Bombay course, which follows Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces closely.
  • Go deeper: a full university lecture (Berkeley CS162) or an expert talk that Hacker News users recommend. The HN count is how many different HN users linked that video.
  • Quick / visual: a short or animated explanation that helps the idea stick.
  • Candidates came from 3,500 YouTube links in Hacker News comments plus YouTube search for every subtopic. High-view exam channels lost when an English lecture explained the same idea more precisely; numericals (Gantt charts, Banker's, page replacement) are covered by the linked MCQs.

subtopics.name: Full courses
subtopics.note: If you have time for one course, take the first. Every best pick below comes from it.

picks.title: Operating Systems (OS) Lectures
picks.why: IIT Bombay course built on OSTEP: 20 concept lectures of 10–30 minutes, then xv6 code walkthroughs showing how a real kernel does traps, context switches, paging and locking.

picks.title: CS162 Spring 2020
picks.why: Berkeley's OS course. Long lectures (80+ minutes) that go further than interviews need on scheduling, deadlock and file systems. Use it for topics you want to master, not as a first pass.

picks.title: Operating Systems Theory
picks.why: Carefully animated explanations of processes, threads, scheduling and IPC. Good for revision once you know the terms.

subtopics.name: OS Basics & Kernel
subtopics.note: Know why there are two privilege modes, what a system call does step by step, and how the OS takes back control of the CPU (timer interrupt).

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 1: Introduction
picks.why: Frames the OS as virtualising the CPU and memory and handling concurrency and persistence: the map that every later topic fits into.

picks.title: CS162 Lecture 2: Four Fundamental OS Concepts
picks.why: Threads, address spaces, processes and dual-mode operation, explained from the hardware up. Watch it when "what happens on a system call" questions feel shaky.

picks.title: How a Single Bit Inside Your Processor Shields Your Operating System's Integrity
picks.why: Animated walk through the mode bit, privileged instructions and traps. Makes user vs kernel mode concrete.

subtopics.name: Processes & fork()
subtopics.note: fork/exec/wait semantics, zombies and orphans, the PCB, and what a context switch saves. The MCQs cover "how many times is this printed" fork puzzles.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 3: System Calls for Process Management
picks.why: fork, exec, wait and exit with real code, including zombies, orphans and how a shell runs a command: exactly what interviewers ask.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 4: Process Execution Mechanisms
picks.why: Limited direct execution: the kernel stack, the trap into the kernel and the context switch, step by step.

picks.title: The Weird Way Linux Creates Processes
picks.why: Why Unix splits creation into fork + exec and how copy-on-write makes it cheap, with clear animation.

subtopics.name: Inter-Process Communication
subtopics.note: Shared memory vs message passing, pipes and named pipes, sockets, and signals. Know the trade-offs, not just the list.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 6: Inter-process communication
picks.why: Shared memory, signals, sockets, pipes and message queues in 12 minutes, each tied to the system calls that create it.

picks.title: Communicating between processes (using pipes) in C
picks.why: Hands-on: pipe() + fork() in C, closing the right ends, and why reads block. Good if you're asked to write it.

picks.title: IPC: To Share Memory Or To Send Messages
picks.why: Visual comparison of the two IPC models and what each costs.

subtopics.name: Threads
subtopics.note: What threads share and what they don't, user vs kernel threads and the 1:1 / M:N models, and why threads help even on one core.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 12: Introduction to threads and concurrency
picks.why: What a thread shares with its process, pthreads basics, and how a data race arises at the instruction level.

picks.title: User-level threads....... with threads. - Paul Turner - Google
picks.why: The most-recommended OS video on Hacker News (20 users). A Google kernel engineer on the real costs of kernel vs user threads and how Google combined them.

picks.title: Why Are Threads Needed On Single Core Processors
picks.why: Clears up the usual confusion between concurrency and parallelism, with animation.

subtopics.name: CPU Scheduling
subtopics.note: FCFS, SJF/SRTF, Round Robin, priority and MLFQ: their metrics (turnaround, waiting, response) and trade-offs. Practise Gantt-chart numericals in the MCQs.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 5: Scheduling Policies
picks.why: FIFO, SJF, STCF, Round Robin and MLFQ with the metric each one optimises, in ten minutes.

picks.title: CS162 Lecture 10: Scheduling 1: Concepts and Classic Policies
picks.why: The same policies with the reasoning behind them: starvation, the convoy effect, and how to compare policies properly.

picks.title: The Fancy Algorithms That Make Your Computer Feel Smoother
picks.why: Animated tour from FCFS to MLFQ and Linux's CFS. Long, but the best visual intuition for why real schedulers look the way they do.

subtopics.name: Process Synchronization
subtopics.note: The most-asked OS topic. Race conditions, how a lock is built from atomic instructions, condition variables (and why you wait in a while loop), semaphores, producer-consumer and readers-writers.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 13: Locks
picks.why: Why disabling interrupts and plain flag variables fail, test-and-set and compare-and-swap, spinning vs sleeping locks.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 14: Condition variables
picks.why: Producer-consumer done correctly with condition variables, including why you re-check the condition in a while loop.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 15: Semaphores
picks.why: Semaphores as locks and as ordering tools, and the bounded-buffer solution.

picks.title: CS162 Lecture 7: Synchronization 2: Semaphores (Con't), Lock Implementation, Atomic Instructions
picks.why: Building locks from atomic instructions and the hardware underneath. Go here for depth on implementation questions.

subtopics.name: Deadlocks
subtopics.note: The four Coffman conditions, prevention by breaking one of them (usually lock ordering), avoidance with Banker's algorithm, and detection.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 16: Concurrency bugs
picks.why: Deadlock conditions and how real code prevents each one, plus atomicity and ordering bugs: the practical side interviewers care about.

picks.title: CS162 Lecture 12: Scheduling 3: Deadlock
picks.why: Full treatment: resource-allocation graphs, detection, and Banker's algorithm worked through.

picks.title: Banker's Algorithm | Operating Systems | GeeksforGeeks
picks.why: A worked safe-sequence example in about four minutes. Watch it before the Banker's MCQs.

subtopics.name: Memory Management & Paging
subtopics.note: Address translation, page tables and multi-level paging, the TLB, segmentation vs paging, and malloc-style free-space management.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 9: Paging
picks.why: Page tables, page-table entries, the TLB and multi-level tables, with the arithmetic for page-table sizes.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 8: Mechanism of address translation
picks.why: Base/bound and segmentation: the problems paging was invented to solve. Watch it first if paging feels arbitrary.

picks.title: Virtual Memory
picks.why: Fourteen short, precise videos (Uppsala University) on translation, page faults, multi-level tables and TLBs, each with worked examples.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 11: Memory allocation and free space management algorithms
picks.why: First/best/worst fit, buddy allocation and slab allocators. Covers "how does malloc work?"

subtopics.name: Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
subtopics.note: Demand paging, what happens on a page fault, FIFO / LRU / Optimal and Belady's anomaly, clock approximation, thrashing and working sets.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 10: Demand Paging
picks.why: The page-fault path, swap, replacement policies, the clock approximation of LRU and thrashing.

picks.title: CS162 Lecture 15: Memory 3: Caching and TLBs (Con't), Demand Paging
picks.why: Demand paging as caching: effective access time, replacement policies and Belady's anomaly, rigorously.

picks.title: SREcon19 Asia/Pacific - Linux Memory Management at Scale: Under the Hood
picks.why: Chris Down (Linux kernel memory developer, Meta) on page cache, reclaim and swap in production. Very good for "how does Linux actually do it" follow-ups.

picks.title: Virtual Memory: 3 What is Virtual Memory?
picks.why: The clearest nine-minute explanation of what virtual memory is for.

subtopics.name: File Systems
subtopics.note: Files, directories and file descriptors, hard vs soft links, inodes and block allocation, and crash consistency with journaling.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 19: File system implementation
picks.why: On-disk layout (superblock, bitmaps, inodes, data blocks), what open/read/write actually touch, caching, and journaling.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 18: Files and directories
picks.why: The file API, the open-file table, hard vs symbolic links: the user-facing half.

picks.title: CS162 Lecture 20 (4/14/2020): Filesystems (Con't), Reliability, Transactions
picks.why: Crash consistency in depth: journaling, copy-on-write file systems and transactions.

subtopics.name: Disk Scheduling & RAID
subtopics.note: Seek, rotation and transfer time; FCFS / SSTF / SCAN / C-SCAN / LOOK; RAID 0, 1, 5 and 10 trade-offs; why SSDs change the picture.

picks.title: Operating Systems Lecture 20: Hard disk internals
picks.why: The disk-access-time model and the scheduling algorithms built on it, in twelve minutes.

picks.title: CS162 Lecture 18 (4/2/2020): Queueing Theory, Disk Scheduling & File Systems
picks.why: Disk scheduling with the queueing theory that explains when it matters.

picks.title: What is RAID 0, 1, 5, & 10?
picks.why: Striping, mirroring and parity, animated in five minutes. Enough for RAID interview questions.

subtopics.name: Virtualization & Linux
subtopics.note: Type 1 vs type 2 hypervisors, trap-and-emulate and hardware support, and containers vs VMs (namespaces + cgroups share one kernel).

picks.title: Virtualization and Cloud Computing Lecture 1: Introduction
picks.why: What a hypervisor must do, the hypervisor types, and where containers fit, from the same IIT Bombay instructor.

picks.title: Cgroups, namespaces, and beyond: what are containers made from?
picks.why: Jérôme Petazzoni builds a container from kernel primitives. After this, "container vs VM" questions are easy.

picks.title: Containers vs VMs: What's the difference?
picks.why: An eight-minute comparison for revision.
